section_summary: This section comprises documentation regarding second-generation Japanese Americans and Canadians (Nisei) residing, studying, and working in Japan during the late 1930s. It begins with a voluntary consular report dated January 29, 1940, prepared by American Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama, which assesses the demographic composition, socio-economic challenges, and Japanese governmental efforts to exploit Nisei residents for pro-Japanese international propaganda during the Sino-Japanese conflict. The remainder of the section contains the main text and survey chapters of Enclosure No. 1, titled 'The Nisei: A Survey of Their Educational, Vocational and Social Problems,' published in October 1939 by the Nisei Survey Committee of Keisen Girls' School in Tokyo, offering statistical and qualitative data on education, employment, lifestyle adjustment, religion, marriage, and dual citizenship.

subfiles.about: A voluntary consular report analyzing the demographic status, living conditions, employment prospects, and Japanese government propaganda exploitation of American citizens of Japanese race residing in Japan.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama, Japan
keywords: Group A and Group B Nisei
subfiles.summary: Consul Richard F. Boyce divides Nisei residing in Japan into two distinct categories: Group A, estimated at 25,000 to 100,000 individuals brought over as young children who are essentially absorbed into Japanese life, and Group B, around 1,500 American-educated youth mainly concentrated in Tokyo for study or work. The report examines the motivations behind their continued stay, highlighting anti-Japanese discrimination and economic limitations in the United States alongside cultural and linguistic challenges in Japan. It documents how the Japanese government, cultural societies, and institutions such as Waseda International Institute sought to utilize Group B Nisei as pro-Japanese goodwill ambassadors and propagandists in radio broadcasting and journalism to sway American public opinion regarding the conflict in China. Boyce concludes that while some Nisei are employed in propaganda capacities, the majority are young students preoccupied primarily with everyday personal and educational adjustment rather than political ideology.
subfiles.title: American Citizens of Japanese Race Residing in Japan

subfiles.about: A comprehensive published survey examining the educational, vocational, social, and citizenship problems confronting North American-born Nisei residing in Tokyo and Yokohama.
subfiles.from: Nisei Survey Committee, Keisen Girls' School, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Conducted by the Summer Class of 1939 at Keisen Girls' School under the guidance of Principal Michi Kawai and supported by the Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai, this study compiles and analyzes questionnaires completed by approximately 440 Nisei in the Tokyo-Yokohama area. The survey details respondents' birthplaces, family backgrounds, and reasons for coming to Japan, finding that the overwhelming majority arrived for educational purposes or accompanied returning parents. It systematically reviews the academic options and difficulties in Japanese schools, vocational openings primarily in foreign trade and clerical work alongside barriers like language limitations and wage levels, and cultural adjustments in domestic life, social etiquette, diet, and religion. Additionally, the booklet addresses dilemmas of dual citizenship, future residential and marriage plans, and concludes with practical advice encouraging prospective Nisei migrants to approach Japan with realistic preparation and open-minded cultural adaptability.
subfiles.title: The Nisei: A Survey of Their Educational, Vocational and Social Problems (Enclosure No. 1)
